newsitem.title: USA: ATHLETICS-SPEEDY NIGHT FOR SPRINTERS AT U.S. CHAMPIONSHIPS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-SPEEDY NIGHT FOR SPRINTERS AT U.S. CHAMPIONSHIPS.

text.p: American sprinters, seemingly in hibernation this spring, roared to life Thursday with stunningly-fast 100-meter times in preliminary rounds at the U.S. championships.

Five men, led by Jon Drummond's 9.92 seconds, ran under 10 seconds in first-round races and Marion Jones produced the year's fastest two women's 100-meter times, dominating the semifinals in 10.92 seconds after running 10.98 seconds in her opening race.
Only seven men have ever run faster than the outspoken Drummond, a 1996 Olympian, and no one has been faster in a non-final.
Headwinds slowed the parade of speedsters in the men's semifinals, where three-time Olympian Dennis Mitchell was eliminated after placing sixth in his race.
The top three finishers in the finals earn a place on the U.S. squad for the Athens world championships in August.
The shot put final was almost as impressive as the 100 meters.

World record-holder Randy Barnes decided the competition with a put of 22.03 meters (72 feet, 3 1/2 inches), the best in 1997. Second went to Kevin Toth with a lifetime best of 21.78 meters (71 feet, 5 1/2 inches) and Olympian C.J. Hunter -- Marion Jones's boyfriend -- claimed third at 21.34 meters (70 feet, 1/4 inch).
World champion John Godina missed a chance to defend his title, placing fourth at 20.49 meters (67 feet, 2 3/4 inches).

Steve Fritz, fourth in the Atlanta Olympics, won the decathlon with 8,604 points, the second-best mark of the year, while Olympian Kelly Blair was first in the heptathlon with a lifetime best of 6,465 points.

The American men had not been among the year's top-five 100-meter runners until Thursday. Maurice Greene changed that with a 9.96-second clocking in the opening heat. Only Trinidad's Ato Boldon, at 9.89 seconds, had run faster.
Drummond came even closer to Boldon's mark with his 9.92 in the third heat. Kareem Streete-Thompson was second at 9.96 seconds.
Also under 10 seconds were Mike Marsh, winner of the fourth heat at 9.97 seconds, and Tim Montgomery, the fifth-heat winner at 9.96 seconds.
The wind shifted into the runners' faces before the men's semifinals and times slowed.
Marsh ran 10.13 seconds and Drummond clocked 10.18 seconds to pace one semifinal. Greene led the second in 10.08.

"I think we are going through a transition where the old guys are getting a little weak, and the young guys like Greene are getting confident and performing well," said Marsh, the 1992 Olympic 200-meter champion. "I came out with the win, and am looking forward to the final tomorrow."

Jones, a former high school star who had concentrated on basketball at the University of North Carolina for the last two years, woke the small crowd with her 10.98-second clocking before the men's races. That improved her personal best by more than a tenth of a second.
Gail Devers, the 1992 Olympic champion, nearly matched Jones by running 10.99 seconds in a later heat. But no one came close to Jones's 10.92-second effort in the semifinals.
"I knew I was ready," said the 21-year-old Jones, who had a wind-assisted clocking of 10.97 seconds earlier this year. "I felt great at 60 meters.
"I did not compete in track last year after breaking my left foot playing basketball, but I'll guarantee you the next few years I'll be in track," she promised.
"I knew if I put in enough time I could be one of the best sprinters in the world."
